lessons.title: Light and electron microscopes
lessons.text:
## Light and electron microscopes
LV: GCSE · Foundation
S: Most cells are too small to see with the naked eye, so almost everything biologists know about cells came from microscopes. Better microscopes, and above all the electron microscope, revealed the tiny structures inside cells.
O: Describe how microscopes developed, from early lenses to the electron microscope
O: Explain the difference between magnification and resolution
O: Compare light and electron microscopes and explain how electron microscopy revealed more sub-cellular structures
REQ: aqa-gcse-biology:4.1.1.5.a @1,3
REQ: aqa-gcse-biology:4.1.1.5.b @2,3
T: Magnification | How many times larger an image appears than the real object
T: Resolution (resolving power) | The ability to see two points that are close together as separate points; higher resolution gives finer detail and a clearer image
T: Micrograph | A photograph of the image seen through a microscope
T: Sub-cellular structure | A structure inside a cell that is smaller than the cell itself, such as a ribosome or mitochondrion
H: Why we need microscopes
P: Typical animal cells are about 0.01 to 0.05 mm across and plant cells about 0.01 to 0.10 mm. The unaided human eye can only make out objects down to about 0.05 mm, so most cells are invisible without help, and the structures inside them are far smaller still.
H: How microscopes developed
- **1590s**: the Janssens, Dutch spectacle makers, tried putting lenses in a tube. These early instruments enlarged things only about 3 to 9 times.
- **1665**: Robert Hooke looked at thin slices of cork with a compound microscope (one with more than one lens). He saw tiny box-like spaces and named them "cells" in his book *Micrographia*.
- **1670s**: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek made microscopes with a single, carefully ground spherical lens that magnified up to about ×275. With them he discovered bacteria and single-celled protozoa.
- **Late 1830s**: Schleiden and Schwann proposed the **cell theory**: living things are made of cells.
- **1800s onwards**: the quality of glass lenses improved, giving sharper images. **Stains** were used to add contrast, because most cells are almost colourless.
- **Electron microscope**: instead of light, it uses a beam of electrons. This allowed biologists to see far smaller structures than any light microscope could.
K: Each improvement in microscopes let biologists see smaller things, from whole cells (Hooke) to bacteria (van Leeuwenhoek) to the structures inside cells (electron microscopes).
H: Magnification and resolution
P: **Magnification** tells you how much bigger the image is than the real object. **Resolution** tells you how much detail you can see: whether two points very close together appear as two points or blur into one.
P: The two are not the same. A light microscope stops being useful beyond roughly ×1000 to ×1500, because enlarging the image further adds no new detail. You just get a bigger blur. To see more, you need better resolution, not just more magnification.
!: Thinking more magnification always shows more detail. Detail depends on resolution; magnifying beyond the resolution limit only makes a blurred image bigger.
!: Sources quote different maximum magnifications for a light microscope (about ×400, ×1000 with oil immersion, or up to about ×1500), depending on the lenses used. Treat it as a range of roughly ×1000 to ×1500 rather than one fixed number.
H: Light and electron microscopes compared
P: Electrons have a much shorter wavelength than light. This is why an electron microscope can resolve much finer detail. A light microscope can separate points about 0.2 µm (200 nm) apart. A modern transmission electron microscope can separate points less than 1 nm apart and can magnify up to about ×1 000 000.
- **Light microscope**: uses light and glass lenses; maximum magnification about ×1000 to ×1500; resolution about 200 nm; can be used to look at living cells; small and relatively cheap.
- **Electron microscope**: uses a beam of electrons; magnification up to about ×1 000 000; resolution below 1 nm; the specimen must be in a vacuum and is prepared in ways that kill it, so living cells cannot be viewed; large and expensive.
- **Transmission electron microscope (TEM)**: the beam passes through a very thin slice of the specimen, showing the structures inside a cell.
- **Scanning electron microscope (SEM)**: the beam scans across the surface, giving a three-dimensional view of the outside of a specimen.
DNEED: Side-by-side comparison of a light microscope and an electron microscope at GCSE level: what each uses to form the image (light and glass lenses, electron beam), with typical maximum magnification and resolution labelled, and the same cell drawn as each would show it (nucleus and mitochondria as blurred shapes under light; ribosomes and mitochondrial inner membranes visible under the electron microscope)
H: What electron microscopy revealed
P: Because of its much better resolving power, the electron microscope showed biologists many structures inside cells for the first time, and showed known structures in detail. **Ribosomes** can only be seen with an electron microscope. **Mitochondria** can be seen with a light microscope, but only as small shapes; the electron microscope shows their internal structure clearly.
K: An electron microscope has far better resolution than a light microscope as well as higher magnification. The better resolution is what lets it reveal sub-cellular structures such as ribosomes and the detail inside mitochondria.
!: Thinking an electron microscope is just a stronger magnifier. Its key advantage is much higher resolving power, which is what reveals new structures.
!: Thinking electron microscopes can show living cells. The vacuum and the preparation of the specimen kill it.
X: Why can a light microscope show mitochondria but not ribosomes?
> Mitochondria are larger than the light microscope's resolution limit of about 200 nm, so they can be seen, though without detail.
> Ribosomes are smaller than that limit, so they cannot be separated from their surroundings however much the image is magnified.
> An electron microscope resolves points less than 1 nm apart, so ribosomes and the inner structure of mitochondria become visible.
H: Using a light microscope
- Thin specimens are placed on a slide and covered with a **coverslip**, which stops the specimen drying out and protects the lens.
- **Stains** add contrast so that colourless parts of a cell show up. Staining usually kills the cells.
SAFE: Handle glass slides and coverslips carefully because they break easily, and follow your teacher's instructions when using stains, as some can irritate skin and eyes.
Q: What is resolution? | The ability to see two points that are close together as separate points.
Q: Why can an electron microscope resolve finer detail than a light microscope? | Electrons have a much shorter wavelength than light.
Q: Which sub-cellular structure can only be seen with an electron microscope? | Ribosomes.
Q: Why can't an electron microscope be used to view living cells? | The specimen must be in a vacuum and is prepared in ways that kill it.
Q: What is the difference between a TEM and an SEM? | A TEM sends the beam through a thin slice to show internal structure; an SEM scans the surface to give a 3D view.
Q: What did Robert Hooke do in 1665? | He looked at cork with a compound microscope and named the small spaces he saw "cells".
M1@1: Which scientist used single-lens microscopes to discover bacteria in the 1670s? | Van Leeuwenhoek | Robert Hooke | Theodor Schwann | Matthias Schleiden | Van Leeuwenhoek's single spherical lenses magnified up to about ×275; Hooke named cells, and Schleiden and Schwann proposed cell theory.
M1@2: What does the resolution of a microscope describe? | How well it separates two close points | How many times it enlarges the image | How bright the image looks to you | How thick a specimen it can view | Resolution is about detail: whether two close points look separate. Enlarging the image is magnification.
M2@2: A student magnifies a light microscope image far beyond ×1500 but sees no new detail. Why? | The image is past the resolution limit | The specimen was not stained enough | The magnification is still too low here | The coverslip blocks the extra detail | Beyond the resolution limit, enlarging only makes the blur bigger; more detail needs better resolution.
M2@3: Which statement correctly compares the two types of microscope? | Only the light type can view living cells | Only the electron type can view living cells | Both types can view living cells clearly | The light type has the better resolution | Electron microscope specimens are placed in a vacuum and prepared in ways that kill them; light microscopes can show living cells.
M3@1,3: Which best explains why biologists learned about ribosomes only after electron microscopes were developed? | Ribosomes are below the light resolution limit | Light microscopes could not magnify above ×10 | Ribosomes are only found in dead cells | Ribosomes cannot be stained for light use | Ribosomes are smaller than about 200 nm, so no light microscope can separate them; electron microscopes resolve below 1 nm.
M3@3: A scientist wants a 3D image of the surface of a pollen grain in fine detail. Which microscope should she use? | A scanning electron microscope | A transmission electron microscope | A light microscope with oil immersion | A light microscope with a strong stain | An SEM scans the surface and gives 3D views at high resolution; a TEM shows internal structure in thin slices.
SA3@2,3: Explain how the electron microscope has increased our understanding of the structures inside cells. | Electron microscopes use electrons, which have a much shorter wavelength than light, so they have much higher resolution (below 1 nm compared with about 200 nm) as well as higher magnification. This means points very close together can be seen as separate, so cells can be studied in much greater detail. Structures too small for a light microscope, such as ribosomes, became visible, and structures such as mitochondria could be seen in detail. | Higher resolution ; Higher magnification ; Links resolution to finer detail ; Names a structure such as ribosomes ; Mitochondria seen in detail
SUM: Microscopes developed from simple lenses in the 1590s to electron microscopes, and each improvement revealed smaller structures.
SUM: Magnification is how much bigger the image is; resolution is how much detail can be seen, and more magnification without better resolution adds no detail.
SUM: Electron microscopes have much higher magnification and resolution than light microscopes, but cannot view living cells.
SUM: The better resolution of electron microscopes revealed sub-cellular structures such as ribosomes and the detail inside mitochondria.

lessons.title: Magnification calculations
lessons.text:
## Magnification calculations
LV: GCSE · Application
S: Biologists measure cells and the structures inside them from micrographs, so you need to link the size of an image, the real size of the object and the magnification. Getting the units right is where most marks are won or lost.
O: Work out the total magnification of a light microscope from its eyepiece and objective lenses
O: Use magnification = image size ÷ real size, rearranged where needed, to find any one of the three values
O: Convert between millimetres, micrometres and nanometres and give answers in standard form
REQ: aqa-gcse-biology:4.1.1.5.c @1,2,3
PRE: Light and electron microscopes
T: Image size | The size of the object as it appears in the image or micrograph
T: Real size | The actual size of the object being viewed
T: Micrometre (µm) | One millionth of a metre, 1 × 10^{-6} m; there are 1000 µm in 1 mm
T: Nanometre (nm) | One thousand-millionth of a metre, 1 × 10^{-9} m
H: The magnification formula
E: magnification = image size ÷ real size :: how many times bigger the image is than the real object
E: real size = image size ÷ magnification :: rearranged to find the real size
E: image size = magnification × real size :: rearranged to find the image size
P: Magnification has no units, because it is one length divided by another. It is often written with a times sign, such as ×400.
P: In a compound light microscope, the total magnification is the eyepiece lens magnification multiplied by the objective lens magnification. For example, an eyepiece of ×10 and an objective of ×40 give 10 × 40 = 400, so the total magnification is ×400.
K: Image size and real size must be in the same unit before you divide. Convert first, then calculate.
H: Units and standard form
- 1 mm = 1000 µm, so to change millimetres to micrometres, multiply by 1000; to change micrometres to millimetres, divide by 1000.
- 1 µm = 1 × 10^{-6} m and 1 nm = 1 × 10^{-9} m.
- A red blood cell about 7 µm across is 7 × 10^{-6} m in standard form.
- Standard form is a number between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of 10. It is useful for very small sizes, such as those of cells and sub-cellular structures.
!: Mixing units, such as dividing an image size in mm by a real size in µm. This gives an answer 1000 times too big or too small and loses marks.
X: A cell in a micrograph is 100 mm long. The real cell is 0.05 mm long. What is the magnification?
> Both lengths are already in mm, so no conversion is needed.
> magnification = image size ÷ real size, so 100 ÷ 0.05 = 2000.
> The magnification is ×2000.
> Check in micrometres: 100 mm is 100000 µm and 0.05 mm is 50 µm, and 100000 ÷ 50 = 2000, the same answer.
X: In a micrograph magnified ×10000, a mitochondrion is 20 mm long. Find its real length in µm and in metres, in standard form.
> real size = image size ÷ magnification, so 20 ÷ 10000 = 0.002 mm.
> Convert to micrometres by multiplying by 1000: 0.002 × 1000 = 2, so the mitochondrion is 2 µm long.
> In metres: 2 µm = 2 × 10^{-6} m.
X: A plant cell 0.08 mm across is viewed through a ×10 eyepiece and a ×40 objective. How wide does it appear in the image?
> Total magnification: 10 × 40 = 400.
> image size = magnification × real size, so 400 × 0.08 = 32.
> The cell appears 32 mm wide.
Q: What is the formula for magnification? | Magnification = image size ÷ real size.
Q: How do you find the total magnification of a light microscope? | Multiply the eyepiece lens magnification by the objective lens magnification.
Q: How many micrometres are in one millimetre? | 1000 µm.
Q: What must you check before dividing image size by real size? | That both are in the same unit.
Q: What is 1 nm in metres, in standard form? | 1 × 10^{-9} m.
M1@1: A microscope has a ×10 eyepiece and a ×40 objective lens. What is the total magnification? | ×400 | ×50 | ×4000 | ×40 | Total magnification is eyepiece × objective, so 10 × 40 = 400. Adding the two gives ×50, adding an extra zero gives ×4000, and ×40 ignores the eyepiece.
M1@3: How many micrometres are there in 0.5 mm? | 500 µm | 5 µm | 50 µm | 5000 µm | There are 1000 µm in 1 mm, so multiply by 1000: 0.5 mm is 500 µm.
M2@2: In a micrograph a cell is 36 mm long. The real cell is 0.012 mm long. What is the magnification? | ×3000 | ×300 | ×0.432 | ×30000 | Magnification = image size ÷ real size, so 36 ÷ 0.012 = 3000. Multiplying the lengths instead gives 0.432.
M2@2: A bacterium appears 12 mm long in an image magnified ×4000. What is its real length? | 0.003 mm | 0.03 mm | 48000 mm | 0.0003 mm | Real size = image size ÷ magnification, so 12 ÷ 4000 = 0.003 mm, which is 3 µm.
M3@2,3: An image of a cell is 40 mm long and the real cell is 20 µm long. What is the magnification? | ×2000 | ×2 | ×0.5 | ×800 | Convert first: 40 mm is 40000 µm, and 40000 ÷ 20 = 2000. Dividing 40 by 20 without converting gives the wrong answer ×2.
M3@3: A structure inside a cell is 0.0004 mm long. What is this in metres, in standard form? | 4 × 10^{-7} m | 4 × 10^{-4} m | 4 × 10^{-6} m | 4 × 10^{-10} m | 0.0004 mm is 0.4 µm, and 1 µm is 1 × 10^{-6} m, so the length is 0.4 × 10^{-6} m, or 4 × 10^{-7} m.
SA3@1,2,3: A student sees a cell through a ×10 eyepiece and a ×10 objective. The image is 5 mm wide. Calculate the real width of the cell in µm, showing your working. | Total magnification = 10 × 10 = 100. Real size = image size ÷ magnification = 5 ÷ 100 = 0.05 mm. Convert to micrometres by multiplying by 1000: 0.05 mm is 50 µm. | Multiplies the lens magnifications to get ×100 ; Uses real size = image size ÷ magnification ; Gets 0.05 mm ; Converts correctly to 50 µm
SUM: Magnification equals image size divided by real size, and the formula can be rearranged to find either size.
SUM: The total magnification of a light microscope is the eyepiece magnification multiplied by the objective magnification.
SUM: Image size and real size must be in the same unit before dividing; 1 mm is 1000 µm.
SUM: Very small sizes are best written in standard form, for example 7 µm is 7 × 10^{-6} m.
